extracted.intended_audience: prospective applicants to NEH Summer Stipends and those who advise them (humanities scholars, independent scholars, faculty at under-served institutions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and writing a competitive NEH Summer Stipends grant application (format, review criteria, narrative content, and common pitfalls). Intended for prospective applicants and their advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual significance of the proposed project
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellectual significance of the proposed project, including its value to humanities scholars, general audiences, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the most important criterion. Explain why the project matters, how it will change the way scholars or other readers understand the topic, and what the research questions are. Put the project in larger scholarly context: note the most important previous work and show how your contribution builds on, disagrees with, or provides a new interpretation. Identify the target audience (scholars, teachers, the public) and explain the payoff of filling any gaps in the literature. Do not oversell (avoid hyperbolic claims like 'transform all scholarship in the humanities'). If revising a dissertation, clearly state what is new and how the project moves beyond the dissertation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of conception, definition, organization, and clarity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of the conception, definition, organization, and description of the project and the applicant’s clarity of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a clear, well-organized narrative that makes sense to non-specialists. Follow suggested outlines in the guidelines if helpful. Use concrete examples to balance abstraction and precision. Avoid jargon or define esoteric terms. Make the document easy to read for panelists who may have many applications to review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility and appropriateness of the proposed plan of work
rubrics_metrics.description: The feasibility and appropriateness of the proposed plan of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a detailed, realistic work plan describing what you will do during the grant period and how it fits into the larger project trajectory. Avoid vague statements like 'spend two months in libraries'; instead specify archives, collections, or concrete activities and demonstrate access (e.g., contact with librarians). Be realistic about what can be achieved in the timeframe—panelists may be skeptical of overly ambitious timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality or promise of quality of the applicant’s work as an interpreter of the humanities
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality or promise of quality of the applicant’s work as an interpreter of the humanities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate your qualifications: previous research and publication record, relevant language skills, training, and access to sources. Explain why you are the right person to carry out the project and show evidence of prior scholarly competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood of project completion and dissemination/access plans
rubrics_metrics.description: The likelihood that the applicant will complete the project (not necessarily during the period of performance), including, when relevant, the soundness of the dissemination and access plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how you will disseminate results (article, book, public programming). If a book, include a brief outline and note any publisher conversations (helpful but not required). Explain how the grant period contributes to overall completion and how audiences will be reached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required application format and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Application components and page limits: three-page narrative, one-page bibliography, two-page CV, any necessary appendices, and names/contact info for two references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application is short; ensure all required pieces are present and conform to page limits. These documents should work together and reinforce each other—treat them as separate chapters of the same case. Include any required supporting materials and the contact information for two references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative element: research and contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative should include discussion of the project’s significance and contribution to the scholarly discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss the scholarly context and most important previous work. State your research questions and explain the unique contribution of your project (what it builds on, disagrees with, or newly interprets). For lesser-known subjects, give extra effort to explain importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative element: methodology and work plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative should describe methodology and the specific work plan for the grant period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how you will answer your research questions and why the chosen methods are appropriate. Identify case studies or sources and describe concrete steps you will take during the grant term. Show evidence you can access needed materials and that the methods will produce the claimed outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative element: competencies, skills, and access
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative should document the applicant’s competencies, language skills, and access to necessary sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail prior work, relevant skills or training, and any arrangements (e.g., archive access, permissions) that show you can carry out the project. This builds confidence in feasibility and applicant suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative element: final product and dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative should state the expected final product and plans for dissemination and access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the intended output (book, article, digital project, public programming) and how it will reach intended audiences. A brief book outline or evidence of publisher interest strengthens the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare early and choose the right program
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan ahead: choose the correct NEH program, read guidelines and samples, register with grants.gov, and contact NEH program officers with questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat grant-seeking as a multi-year process. Confirm eligibility and fit with the program. Register and familiarize yourself with grants.gov well before the deadline. Review sample successful applications to understand structure and form. Program officers can answer questions but cannot read drafts for this program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your case and explicitly address review criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure your narrative to start from the review criteria and explicitly demonstrate how your project meets them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may explicitly flag criteria in the narrative (e.g., 'This project is significant because...'; 'I will disseminate this research by...'). Doing so helps evaluators find the information they are asked to consider. Emphasize significance, context, and a clear work plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience awareness: write for both specialists and generalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Write so that both disciplinary specialists and non-specialist panelists can understand the project’s significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid in-group jargon or define specialized terms. Provide enough context so generalists grasp why the project matters to specialists. Use concrete examples to illustrate arguments and balance broad claims with specific evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to details: draft early, solicit feedback, and proofread
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention to bureaucratic and formal details: draft early, get feedback (especially from non-specialists), update bibliography, include required supporting materials, and proofread thoroughly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit comments from colleagues and mentors, including those outside your subfield. Keep your bibliography current so panelists see you know the literature. Proofread to avoid distracting errors. Do not submit last-minute to avoid technical or registration issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference letters should support the project’s significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters of reference should focus on the project and its significance rather than only on the applicant’s past accomplishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss the project with letter writers and send them the application and criteria so they can advocate effectively. If the project spans disciplines, consider letters from scholars in each relevant field. Ensure letter writers are familiar with the project to avoid letters that explain the project better than the application itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-decision actions: request comments and resubmit if necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If not funded, request reviewers’ comments, contact a program officer for clarification, and revise and resubmit your application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review panel comments carefully and use them to strengthen resubmissions. Program officers can help interpret comments and advise about resubmission strategy. Experience shows resubmissions are often more successful after clarifying and improving the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common errors to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical faults seen in unsuccessful applications: ignoring the guidelines; not making the case for significance; focusing merely on gaps in scholarship without payoff; fuzzy methodology; incomplete or vague work plan; using jargon; not moving beyond the dissertation; unhelpful reference letters; not planning ahead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the guidelines closely and tailor the application to NEH expectations. Make a clear case for significance and explain the payoff of filling gaps. Provide concrete methodology and a developed work plan (show access to archives if applicable). Avoid jargon and explain novelty beyond a dissertation. Ensure reference letters address the project’s importance. Plan your timetable early to allow for drafting, feedback, and technical submission through grants.gov.
